name.text: Solving an equation with the identity step by step

questiontext.text:
Solve \({@eqd@}\) for \(0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ\).

(a) Let \(c = \cos x\). Write the equation as a quadratic equation in \(c\).

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Write the set of values of \(c\) that can be values of \(\cos x\).

\(c \in\) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

(c) Write the set of solutions \(x\). Give angles that are not whole numbers to 1 decimal place.

\(x \in\) [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]] [[feedback:prt3]]

generalfeedback.text:
Change every ratio into the same ratio: then it is a quadratic you already know how to solve.

(a) Replace \(\sin^2 x\) by \(1 - \cos^2 x = 1 - c^2\):

\[{@p@}(1 - c^2){@tm(q, "c")@}{@tc(r)@} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad {@tq@} = 0.\]

(b) The roots are \(c = {@cv@}\) and \(c = {@cb@}\). But \(\cos x\) can never be bigger than 1 or smaller than \(-1\), so \(\cos x = {@cb@}\) is impossible. So \(c \in \{{@cv@}\}\).

(c) [[if test="is(cv = 1)"]]\(\cos x = 1\) gives \(x = 0^\circ\) and \(x = 360^\circ\): both ends of the interval count.[[else]]\(\cos x = {@cv@}\): your calculator gives \(\alpha = {@degraw(al)@}\). Cosine has the same value at \(360^\circ - \alpha\).[[/if]] So \(x \in {@setraw(sols)@}\).

questiondescription.text:
Trigonometry III: solving with the identity step by step

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.5: Solve p sin^2 x + q cos x + r = 0 for 0 to 360 degrees: the quadratic in cos x, the valid values of cos x, then the angles.

Core

This question is adapted from E2, E3 and Question 2 in Exercise E of Chapter 7 of Cassell, D., Instone, S., Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP AS/A2 Mathematics: Core 2 for AQA, Cambridge University Press, 2004: new equations in degrees with a rejected root in every variant, randomised over a curated list, the steps scaffolded and named feedback added.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: You replaced \(\sin^2 x\) by \(1 - \cos x\). It is \(1 - \cos^2 x = 1 - c^2\).

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(qdeg # 2)"]]

Part (a) asks for a quadratic equation in \(c\), with a \(c^2\) term; solving it comes in (b).

[[/if]]

Replace \(\sin^2 x\) by \(1 - c^2\), multiply out and collect the terms on one side.

truefeedback.text: These are the two roots of the quadratic, but one of them cannot be a value of \(\cos x\): \(-1 \le \cos x \le 1\) for every angle. Leave it out.

node.sans: matchset(cl, float(lrv), 0.001) and not isprop(pe, tq) and is(lrv # [])

truefeedback.text: These are the right values for your quadratic in (a), but (a) is not right, so they are not the values for this equation.
Close, but give the exact value of \(c\), as a fraction such as 2/3, not a rounded decimal.

falsefeedback.text: Factorise the quadratic from (a) (or use the formula) and keep only the values between \(-1\) and \(1\).

truefeedback.text: Test your second angle on a calculator: \(\cos {@degraw(180-al)@} = {@-cv@}\), not \({@cv@}\). The rule \(180^\circ - \alpha\) is for sine; use the symmetry of the cosine graph.
These angles solve the equation you get with the sign slip \(\sin^2 x = c^2 - 1\) in (a).

node.sans: matchset(sl, ftangF, 0.0501) and is(ftangF # []) and not matchset(cl, [float(cv)], 0.001)

truefeedback.text: Your angles are right for your values of \(c\) in (b), but (b) is not right.

Every angle you gave is a solution, but the equation has {@length(solsF)@} solutions in \(0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ\) and you gave {@length(sl)@}.[[if test="miss360"]] When \(0^\circ\) is a solution, \(360^\circ\) is one too: both ends are in the interval.[[/if]]

[[if test="is(extras = [])"]]You have every solution, but you gave at least one of them twice, to different accuracy. Give each angle once.[[else]]You have every solution, but also {@setstr(extras)@}.[[/if]][[if test="is(outside # [])"]] Angles outside \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) are not wanted: add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring a calculator value into the interval.[[/if]]

Each of your angles is close to a solution, but not correct to 1 decimal place. Keep full calculator accuracy and round only at the end, to 1 decimal place (round up when the next digit is 5 or more).

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(resx # [])"]]

Test your angles in the equation. For the left side of the equation, {@resstr@}. A solution gives \(0\).

[[/if]]

Each solution makes \(\cos x\) equal to the value of \(c\) from (b): your calculator gives one angle \(\alpha\); find the other from the symmetry of the cosine graph.

[[if test="is(outside # [])"]]

Angles outside \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) are not wanted: add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring a calculator value into the interval.

[[/if]][[if test="radn"]]

All your values are small: check that your calculator is in degree mode, and give angles in degrees.

[[/if]]
